summary:
Sam Bhagwat opens by framing the agents-vs-workflows debate as unnecessarily polarized, referencing Anthropic's December 'Building Effective Agents' blog post and OpenAI's April paper criticized for an anti-workflow stance. He offers two hot takes. First, 'don't be that guy'—criticizing dogmatic pronouncements from influential providers, comparing them to Googlers who lectured web developers about platform correctness. He urges model providers to elevate discourse quality given their outsized ecosystem influence. Second, he considers graph node-and-edge terminal APIs harmful, arguing teams shouldn't need graph theory knowledge to build workflows. He contrasts these with fluent syntax that reads top-to-bottom, using Mastra's workflow syntax as an example, and draws an analogy to Gatsby.js's GraphQL default that alienated users.

He references Christopher Alexander's 1970s architectural pattern catalogs, noting the field still lacks commonly accepted terminology for agentic and workflow patterns. He defines agents as turn-based games with back-and-forth tool calls and workflows as rules engines for dependency chains, likening them to Civilization-style tech trees. Emergent agent properties include conversation threads and memory; workflow properties include branching, parallelism, conditions, loops, suspension, resuming, and replaying. Workflows matter more in AI engineering because non-determinism makes tracing and debugging far more critical than in traditional software engineering.

He frames the choice as a power-versus-control trade-off: start with power, add structure where reliability falters. He describes whiteboarding sessions where teams break underperforming single LLM calls into multiple structured calls. He then details composition patterns with concrete examples: a research agent, summary agent, and orchestrator agent working together; workflows as tools (e.g., plan location, check weather, plan a trip passed to an agent for iteration); workflows performing agent handoffs; dynamic tool injection (agents can fail with double-digit tool counts, so be selective); and nested workflows. He emphasizes that the real value comes from combining these patterns together, and that production agentic workflows contain surprising amounts of detail. In Q&A, he stresses that the community is practice-driven, not theory-driven—if an agent works with 20 tools, do it; if theory disagrees, the theory may be wrong. The field is young and practice is evolving faster than theory.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

takeaways: The agents-vs-workflows debate is a false dichotomy; teams should combine both primitives flexibly.
Model providers should avoid dogmatic pronouncements given their outsized ecosystem influence.
Graph node-and-edge APIs are harmful because they require graph theory knowledge and reduce code readability.
Agents resemble turn-based games with back-and-forth tool calls; workflows resemble dependency-driven rules engines.
Workflows are especially valuable in AI engineering due to non-determinism, making tracing and debugging critical.
The power-vs-control trade-off lets you start flexible and add structure where reliability fails.
Agents and workflows compose: an agent can be a step, a workflow can be a tool, agents can supervise other agents, and workflows can do agent handoffs.
Dynamic tool injection matters—agents can fail when given double-digit numbers of tools, so be selective about which tools to provide.
The real value comes from combining composition patterns together; production agentic workflows contain surprising detail.
The AI agent field is a community of practice more than theory; if your approach works, use it even if theory disagrees.

sections.title: Introduction and Debate Context
sections.summary: Sam introduces himself as co-founder of Gatsby.js and Mastra, author of Principles of AI Agents. He frames the agents-vs-workflows debate, referencing Anthropic's December 'Building Effective Agents' blog post and OpenAI's controversial April paper with an anti-workflow callout that sparked Twitter debate and a Latent Space blog post.

sections.title: Don't Be That Guy: Critiquing Provider Dogma
sections.summary: Hot take #1: model providers shouldn't be dogmatic. Bhagwat compares big provider pronouncements to certain Googlers who lectured web devs about 'the right way' to use platforms, urging elevated discourse quality given providers' outsized influence.

sections.title: Harmful APIs and the Case for Fluent Syntax
sections.summary: Hot take #2: graph node-and-edge terminal APIs are harmful. Teams shouldn't need graph theory to build workflows. Bhagwat prefers fluent syntax readable top-to-bottom, using Mastra workflows as an example, and draws a Gatsby/GraphQL analogy where defaulting to an unfamiliar pattern alienated users.

sections.title: Design Patterns and the Need for Shared Language
sections.summary: References Christopher Alexander's 1970s architectural pattern catalog that software engineers adopted. Notes the AI field still lacks commonly accepted verbiage and glossary for agentic and workflow patterns.

sections.title: Defining Agents and Workflows
sections.summary: Defines agents as turn-based games with back-and-forth tool calls and workflows as rules engines for dependency chains (like Civilization tech trees). Agent emergent properties: conversation threads, memory. Workflow emergent properties: branching, parallelism, conditions, loops, suspend/resume/replay. Workflows matter more in AI engineering due to non-determinism.

sections.title: Trade-offs, Whiteboarding, and Reliability
sections.summary: Frames the choice as power-vs-control trade-off: start with power, add structure where things fail. Describes whiteboarding sessions where teams break underperforming single LLM calls into multiple structured calls for reliability, e.g., splitting 12-symptom medical PDF diagnosis into 12 calls.

sections.title: Composition Patterns and Concrete Examples
sections.summary: Details composition patterns with code examples: research agent, summary agent, orchestrator agent. Workflows as tools (plan location, check weather, plan trip passed to an agent). Workflows doing agent handoffs. Dynamic tool injection—agents can fail with double-digit tool counts. Nested workflows. Emphasizes the real value comes from combining patterns together, and that production agentic workflows have surprising detail.

sections.title: Q&A and Concluding Thoughts
sections.summary: Q&A covers combining deep research agents with known workflows and agents working with 20 tools. Bhagwat stresses the community is practice-driven, not theory-driven: if it works, do it; if theory disagrees, theory may be wrong. The field is young and practice evolves faster than theory. He invites attendees to find him at the conference (handle: calcam) and grab a copy of his book.
